reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The patient cohorts/databases used should be better described in detail. E.g. how was the diagnosis Covid-19 made in these databases (SARS-CoV-2 PCR proven? diagnostic criteria?). Also include details on composition, quality of data used in manuscript, access etc.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified inclusion was based on positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR/RNA test, COVID-19 ICD codes, or both; reported that 6.31% of Optum diagnoses lacked a recorded positive test and noted CovEWS performance was robust in a later Optum Future cohort where all diagnoses had positive tests.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A major limitation is the fact that by far the most patients are included before treatment protocols were changed around the world to exclude antibiotics and include remdesivir, dexamethasone and anticoagulant therapy... It is thought that current overall mortality is less when compared to situations of a first wave/first responders in this pandemic. The authors address this in a limited fashion by having a secondary analysis in patients that presented in July. At the very least this should be highlighted in the limitation section.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors evaluated CovEWS on an Optum Future cohort recruited after RECOVERY trial results were reported and showed performance was sustained despite treatment changes; added reasoning for robustness to treatment-pattern changes (percentile-based risk score remains robust to absolute mortality probability shifts).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper describes the development, validation and performance of the CovEWS tool, but gives limited attention to the practical aspects and limitations of this tool... Could you elaborate on how you plan to introduce this tool into clinical practice and what specific steps are needed to prove the benefits of the tool?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added discussion of two deployment options (standalone web app and EHR-integrated solution), and outlined future RCT to evaluate impact on resource use and outcomes.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Could you elaborate on why you chose to present the mortality risk in a 0-100 percentile range? This reviewer believes that it would be hard to translate such a number into a clinical action. An absolute mortality risk could be much clearer.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained that percentile-based score avoids misleading direct probability interpretation, is robust across prediction horizons, and is stable under shifts in absolute mortality due to treatment changes.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the results section, an excellent overview of the performance of the CovEWS in relation to other predictors of mortality is given in figure 1. However, the comparison with the SOFA score has some limitations. The SOFA score is based on an intensive care population and should thus do much better in patient A than in patient B. This reviewer feels that a comparison with the MEWS would be more insightful. The limitation of the SOFA score should at least be acknowledged in this regard.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added MEWS (Modified Early Warning Score) as an additional comparator in Figures 1 and 3 and supplementary tables.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It was unclear how to make fair comparisons when there exist a huge number of missing variables. For instance, there are more than 99% values of hs-CRP (one of key variables in [17]) missing in the external validation dataset. ... CovEWS demanded high dimensional inputs for mortality prediction... It is expected that the prediction accuracy will drop significantly if a large number of factors are missing.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified MICE estimators were derived from the training set only (Optum) and applied to other folds/datasets; noted hs-CRP can be accurately imputed from highly-correlated CRP; argued evaluation under realistic missingness is fairer than complete-case analysis.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: TriNetX dataset was selected for the external validation in this study. A significant concern about this study is the generalizability. The model performance on this external dataset seems not optimal (even the author explained the missing value problem). Especially, results in the time-varying plot in Figure 3 show that only about 50% of the identified high-risk patients (CovEWS score is 90-100 indicating a very high mortality risk) eventually died. The authors should consider if TriNex is an appropriate dataset for generalizability analysis and explicitly discuss the impact of missing variables.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors defended TriNetX as appropriate precisely because it tests robustness across geography, population and missingness; noted CovEWS still significantly outperformed all other scoring systems on TriNetX.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Baseline methods from Yan et al. and Liang et al. show promising results in their studies. However, these studies were done at the initial breakout of COVID-19 with fewer patient samples and most of the patients were Asian. Without re-training or re-tuning these models with datasets used in this study, it is unfair to say the model proposed in this study is superior to these methods.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors argued it is appropriate to independently evaluate published models on a larger more representative cohort precisely because original cohorts were small and non-representative; noted none of the compared methods including CovEWS were retrained on the external TriNetX cohort.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: When splitting the dataset, the authors wrote: 'To demonstrate the generalizability of predictions made by CovEWS, we limited the training of CovEWS to a training cohort of 14 215 (30%) patients from the Optum cohort, used 9 477 (20%) Optum patients for model selection, and evaluated CovEWS against both a held-out test cohort of 14 215 (30%) patients from the Optum cohort.' What about the rest 20% patients?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged the percentage error; clarified that training cohort actually corresponded to 23,692 patients (50%) and corrected the manuscript.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The CovEWS model itself is not interpretable since the authors applied neural networks to enhance feature learning ability of the model. To address this issue, the developed CovEWS model identified clinically-relevant factors for mortality prediction using the Integrated Gradient method (IG). Importance of different factors can be ranked based on the scores produced by IG. However, it seems that this approach cannot provide detailed threshold for these factors in order to set up clinical warning in practice.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained warnings should be set on patient-level CovEWS score thresholds rather than per-feature thresholds; pointed to the manuscript's threshold section (S.10).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The use of ICD-9/10 codes as a predictor is not clinically useful. Physicians never code their diagnosis - most of diagnoses are coded after admission or discharge. How does the clinician use the model?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors stated that diagnostic codes are only used from the time they were entered into the EHR (i.e., predictive performance reflects real-world coding timing); reported that 85.0% (TriNetX) and 72.5% (Optum) of diagnoses were coded and available before patient inclusion based on COVID-19 diagnosis/test.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The definition of outcome (death) is not validated. In addition to the non-validated study population (i.e. COVID-19 diagnosis), the uncertainty in death may bias the results.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors noted mortality outcomes were validated at source by healthcare organizations; acknowledged systematic bias from outpatient deaths possibly being missed; added limitation about incomplete outpatient death records.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The lack of prospective evaluation limits the generalizability/transportability. In general, the lack of generalizability/transportability is more problematic when using claims data.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors pointed to evaluation on the TriNetX cohort (5,005 patients, 24 HCOs, international) and a temporally-separated Optum Future cohort; argued these demonstrate generalization to new environments and conditions.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I was not convinced by the performance and comparison results using datasets that has more than 99.28% missing measurements for one of the key variables used in different models. In other words, there is only 1 in every 140 patients that has a measurement. How can one infer/estimate the measurements of other patients based on this single measurement? ... MICE is good for imputing missing values... But there is a more fundamental problem before applying MICE: what is the largest percentage that MICE can impute with a trustable performance? When the ratio of missing values exceeds this threshold, the imputed values become random guess. Then the conclusion drawn could be wrong!
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified the 99.28% missingness is in the external TriNetX test set; the MICE estimator was learned on training set (Optum, 96.62% missingness in hsCRP, but still ~800 patients available); argued that percentage missingness is not the relevant threshold and that imputation quality depends on cross-covariate associations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: My previous concerns on the fairness of comparison using largely missing datasets still hold. There are too many missing values for variables in ALL compared models. Using, for instance, values of CRP to estimate those of hs-CRP is not a good idea. Not only they have different means, they have different impact (Table S4). One shall notice that the p-values were calculated using chi-squared tests are different (0.52 versus < 0.005).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors enumerated 4 evaluation options (impute on all, withhold predictions, complete-case only, no comparison) and defended their chosen approach; added 6 sub-cohort analyses with fewer missing covariates showing rankings sustained.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Three reviewers, three rounds (round 1, round 2 R2 mostly unsatisfied + R3 satisfied + R1 satisfied; round 3 R2 satisfied). Strong methodological focus throughout, especially on missingness, MICE validity, and external validation under distribution shift. C06/C07/C14/C15 are the same thread (Reviewer #2's persistent missingness concern across rounds) — kept separate to track resolution dynamics. Missingness thread never formally resolved by reviewer in round 3 text — reviewer simply moves on. Author response style is rebuttal-heavy with frequent disagreement.

Pure CT imaging study: deep CNN (U-Net x3) for coronary artery calcium segmentation/scoring from gated and non-gated cardiac CT, then linking CAC scores to cardiovascular events. CLAUDE.md explicitly excludes imaging from MLGG scope. Reviewer concerns center on segmentation Dice, U-Net design, tile/cube sizes, novelty vs prior CNN-CAC literature — not applicable to MLGG's retrospective EHR/registry binary classification gates.

Histopathology whole-slide image (WSI) classification of lung cancer subtypes using unified-memory CNN with slide-level labels. CLAUDE.md explicitly excludes imaging. Reviewer concerns are about WSI tiling, MIL baselines, GPU memory, magnification levels — image-modality specific, not MLGG-applicable.

Multi-task deep learning on longitudinal multi-parametric MRI (T1+C, T2WI, DWI) for rectal cancer pCR prediction with simultaneous segmentation. Pure medical imaging modality — out of MLGG scope per CLAUDE.md. Reviewer concerns are about MRI sequence selection, COMBAT harmonization, tumor contouring kappa, Dice — image-pipeline specific.

Integrated multi-omics analysis (bulk RNASeq n=535, CNV/LOH SNP array n=473, spatial proteomics n=167) of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer. CLAUDE.md explicitly excludes omics (TCGA/scRNA/GWAS) from MLGG scope. Reviewer concerns focus on RNASeq somatic mutation calling validity, germline filtering, transcriptomic class delineation — properly handled by Scanpy/limma/bioinformatics tooling, not MLGG.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: ICD coding for wild-type amyloid was used as the gold standard - this is flawed as we do not know what the specific ECG, imaging, and histology findings are for these patients, or what criteria was used to make this diagnosis. Even within wild-type amyloid there are many different genetic variants all with different phenotypes, and the authors fail to tease this out as their ICD coding was purely 'wild-type'. ... Similarly, 'heart failure' is very broad term and is often miscoded. Further, it is HFPEF that we are interested in, and not just any heart failure.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors disagreed that wild-type ATTR has genetic variants (by definition it is diagnosed in absence of TTR variants); disagreed that only HFpEF is relevant (citing ATTR-ACT data showing 22% HFrEF, 29% HFmrEF, 50% HFpEF); acknowledged HF code limitation in discussion text.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: NRI and IDI was calculated and at least one should be included in the results.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added IDI=0.039 (95% CI 0.031-0.048) p<0.00001 and category-less NRI=0.25 (95% CI 0.22-0.28) p<0.00001 to results, indicating ML algorithm improved over conventional predictors.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The biggest concern is that that a sizable number of the controls may have undiagnosed amyloidosis. The authors mention it as a limitation in the 'limitations' paragraph, but that is not sufficient. They should address it in the results/discussion and discuss how using models with higher specificity in this instance may be inferior to those with higher sensitivity.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added discussion noting future prospective studies with systematic application of gold standard tests will be needed for further development and validation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the model described page 10, how did they deal with the differential use of BNP and NT-proBNP and differential use of troponin I, troponin T, and hs-troponin T? Definition of high is different in Text and in Table 5 legend (0.4 in former and 0.04 in latter). The latter is correct for abnormal whereas the former is not.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified Northwestern uses a single assay (BNP not NTproBNP, troponin I not troponin T) so assays were uniform; corrected troponin threshold typo to >0.04 ng/ml.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The obvious point - the model performance is predicated upon assignment of cases and controls. We can presume for the sake of argument that cases of ATTRwt-CM are likely to be accurate. But similar to the point made in the discussion regarding the NW dataset, there definitively unrecognized cases of ATTRwt-CM in the control cohort. ... ideally the negative controls should come from a cohort who have all undergone PYP scintigraphy (which all but excludes cardiac ATTR amyloidosis). Given that this undoubtedly compromises the assessment of accuracy of the algorithm, the editors may wish to consider requesting the addition of a more fully characterised control cohort.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged the limitation; stated they are not aware of large-scale cohorts of HF patients consecutively examined with confirmatory PYP scintigraphy; framed the algorithm as a starting point to stimulate such studies.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The responses to reviewer #4 are acceptable. I do strongly encourage to not perpetuate the use of AUROC as a metric in such situations and instead focus on AUPRC values, the increase in post-test PPV etc. It does us all a disservice to play up AUROC, and numbers in the 80s, when they are practically useless in the use case envisioned and for low prevalence events can misguide a lot of readers.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors removed AUROC listings from the abstract; opted to keep AUROC in body with positive/negative likelihood ratios (Table 5) rather than adding AUPRC (citing clinician interpretability concerns).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: However that increased case finding ability needs to be balanced with the harm that will be inflicted on the false positives. Will they be tested with a 'confirmatory test'? How much does that cost, is it invasive? And net-net what is the number needed to test (and $$ needed to spend) to find one new case of ATTR-CM, which we are currently missing. That kind of discussion is essential.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added discussion of downstream confirmatory testing pathway (light-chain blood/urine tests, PYP scintigraphy, endomyocardial biopsy, TTR genetic testing) and noted formal cost-effectiveness analysis is outside scope but warranted.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Authors have made a valiant effort to address the limitations cited by the previous reviewers. There is indeed value to this paper in potentially screening the population for Wild-type TTR Amyloidosis, however, I do agree with previous reviewers' suggestions that 'the algorithm only flags individuals potentially at-risk for wild-type ATTR-CM but does not diagnose the condition'. This is not forthcoming and the manuscript title and results may mislead a reader. ... I would tone down all throughout the manuscript carefully any claims towards diagnosis and early detection of ATTRwt-CM.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors changed title to 'A Machine Learning Model of Medical Claims Data for Identifying Patients at Risk for Wild-Type Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy'; revised discussion to emphasize 'targeted testing and confirmation' rather than 'diagnosis and early detection'.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Editorial note: manuscript was previously reviewed at another journal (so reviewers #2,#5,#6,#7 are inherited from prior submission); subsequent round at Nature Comms added reviewers #7,#8,#9. Five distinct reviewers (#2,#5,#6,#7,#9) provided substantive comments in this PDF. Two rounds at Nature Communications. Dominant theme: case/control label fidelity given ICD-only ascertainment (C01, C03, C05) - flagged CRITICAL because the model is trained against a non-validated outcome. Reviewer #7's AUROC critique for low-prevalence events maps cleanly to MLGG-E02.

Genomic resource (Pathogenwatch) for whole-genome-sequence-based AMR prediction and phylogenetic surveillance of Salmonella Typhi. Pathogen genomics / WGS / phylogenetics — out of MLGG scope (omics-adjacent; should use pathogen bioinformatics tooling). Reviewer concerns focus on contig filtering, tree topology, MIC vs SIR data, web app usability — not applicable to MLGG's retrospective EHR binary-classification gates.

Deep learning CNN on low-dose chest CT volumes (NLST, MGH cohorts) to predict cardiovascular disease and CVD mortality from lung-cancer-screening LDCT images. Pure medical imaging modality — out of MLGG scope per CLAUDE.md. Reviewer concerns are about CT-specific issues (scan protocols, reconstruction kernels, motion artifacts, slice fusion via max-pooling), not MLGG-applicable EHR/tabular gates.

Deep learning system for diabetic retinopathy detection across disease spectrum from retinal fundus images, with multi-task lesion detection. Pure retinal-imaging modality — out of MLGG scope. Note: the split-by-district concern (Reviewer #1, 'Data splits') is methodologically interesting and would map to split_protocol_gate in principle, but the overall paper is an imaging study so we mark OUT_OF_SCOPE on the wholistic recheck rule rather than cherry-picking one concern from an out-of-scope modality.

Plasma proteomic profiling (DIA-MS, ~500 proteins) plus SARS-CoV-2 RNAemia plus pulldown experiments for ICU COVID-19 prognostication. Proteomics-dominant study — out of MLGG scope (omics). The ML component is a small SVM on Age+PTX3 mentioned by reviewers; not the primary analysis. Reviewer concerns focus on serum/plasma protocol consistency, MS data analysis methods, PTX3 specificity, IP/pulldown controls — not MLGG-applicable.
